A **cyclin** in cell biology drives the cell cycle forward: **cyclin D1 binds CDK4/6 to phosphorylate Rb**, releasing E2F to transcribe genes for G1-to-S transition. That's proliferation, not death.

You are building the right bridge, but let me tighten the tracks.

In Huntington's, **mutant huntingtin disinhibits the striatum** — the GABA breaks are off, so the thalamus is always pressing the gas. That is a **loss of inhibition** driving excess movement.

In pituitary Cushing, **autonomous ACTH is the finger that never lifts off the button**. The adrenal cortex receives continuous ligand, so **cAMP → PKA is always on**, driving unrelenting cortisol synthesis. No diurnal dip. No feedback shutoff.

The mechanistic mirror: both are **pathways stuck in the "on" position** — one from lost brakes (Huntington), one from a stuck accelerator (Cushing). But the molecules are different: **GNAS is the stuck G protein itself** (McCune-Albright), while **this patient has a stuck ligand** (ACTH) driving a normal G protein.

The bedside anchor: **bilateral adrenal hyperplasia** tells you the accelerator is being pressed from above, not stuck inside the gland.

**Prompt for a 1x4 grid, top-down view, cinematic medical illustration style:**

"Top-down schematic view, four panels side by side, labeled 1 through 4. Each panel shows a signaling pathway as a straight horizontal track from left to right. Panel 1: **Normal brake and accelerator** — a hand presses a green button labeled 'ligand' briefly, then lifts; downstream a 'cortisol' gauge rises then falls. Panel 2: **Stuck ligand (Pituitary Cushing)** — a hand presses the same green button and never lifts; the cortisol gauge is pinned to max, bilateral adrenal glands glow red and enlarged. Panel 3: **Stuck G protein (McCune-Albright)** — the hand is absent, but the button is replaced by a jammed Gs alpha subunit icon; the cortisol gauge is pinned, adrenal glands glow but asymmetrically. Panel 4: **Lost brake (Huntington)** — the track shows a GABA neuron as a red stop sign that is shattered; downstream a movement gauge is pinned to max, striatum glows hyperactive. Color palette: cold blue for normal, hot red for stuck-on states. Arrow icons show continuous activation flow. Clean, top-down, no perspective, white background."

That captures **three mechanisms — stuck ligand, stuck G protein, lost brake — all driving the same outcome: a pathway that cannot turn off.**
